before: A comma separates alternative selectors: .note, .urgent matches elements with either class. With no space or comma, .note.urgent matches one element that has both classes. HTML separates multiple class names using spaces.

The period introduces each class selector. Joining two class selectors with no separator adds requirements on the same element. Adding a space would instead describe a descendant relationship. The declarations inside braces apply to every matching element, regardless of how many alternatives it matches.

Make only the paragraph with both note and urgent classes teal. Keep the other two navy. The supplied HTML stays in index.html; edit the CSS. The checks inspect this small page, not every possible browser or accessibility requirement.
after: A comma separates choices in a selector list. `.note, .urgent` chooses any part with the `note` class or the `urgent` class. A part with both classes also matches.

Joining class selectors means the same part must have both classes. `.note.urgent` needs `note` and `urgent` on one part. HTML writes those class names with a space: `class="note urgent"`. A space inside the CSS selector has a different job: it looks for a part inside another part.
The order of class names in HTML does not matter. `class="urgent note"` still has the two names needed by `.note.urgent`. Run the project and check that only this paragraph is teal.

before.question: An element has class="urgent note" instead of class="note urgent". Does .note.urgent still match?
choices: Only a comma selector can match multiple classes.
Yes; both class names are present.
No; class attributes must use the selector’s order.
before.explanation: Class membership is not an ordered sequence. The compound selector requires both names, not a particular order.

after.question: The HTML uses class="urgent note". Does .note.urgent still match?
choices: Only a selector with a comma can match two classes.
Yes. Both class names are present.
No. The names must be in the same order.
after.explanation: Both names are present. Their order in the HTML does not change which classes the element has.
